The most common pure form of testicular cancer is seminoma, a type of germ cell tumor which is radiosensitive.

Risk factors: cryptorchidism (3 to 8 times; the risk persists after orchidopexy), a family history (father or brother), a previous testicular cancer (contralateral), infertility, HIV, hypospadias, carcinoma in situ, in-utero exposure (DES), and Klinefelter's syndrome.
Improved survival with early detection + access to standard regimens (e.g. childhood ALL, testicular cancer – highly curable even in resource-limited settings if treated properly)
Cryptorchidism — undescended testis; 3–5× ↑ testicular cancer risk (via intratubular germ cell neoplasia); orchiopexy reduces risk

qs.q: A patient with testicular cancer is treated with a platinum compound that frequently causes significant nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity. Which drug is this?
qs.e: Cisplatin is a platinum compound well-known for causing severe nephrotoxicity that requires aggressive hydration, as well as ototoxicity. Carboplatin is notably less nephrotoxic than cisplatin.

qs.q: A 30-year-old male is investigated for infertility and a history of cryptorchidism corrected during childhood. What is the approximate magnitude of increased testicular cancer risk associated with cryptorchidism?
qs.e: Cryptorchidism confers a 3 to 5 fold increased risk of developing testicular cancer and is present in approximately 10 percent of all testicular cancer cases. A family history involving affected brothers increases risk by 8 to 10 fold.
